The Fibonacci sequence. It is the integer sequence defined by the recurrence F of n equals F of n minus one plus F of n minus two, with F of one equals one and F of two equals one. This yields the sequence one, one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen, twenty-one, and so on. This seemingly simple recurrence produces numbers ubiquitous in nature: spiral seed arrangements in sunflowers, the branching of trees, the spirals of shells. It connects to the golden ratio, making it one of the most recognizable sequences in mathematics.

The Fibonacci sequence grows exponentially. F of n is approximately phi to the n divided by the square root of five, where phi equals one plus the square root of five divided by two, the golden ratio. The ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers, F of n plus one divided by F of n, converges to the golden ratio, approximately one point six one eight. Fibonacci numbers appear hidden in Pascal's triangle: the diagonals sum to Fibonacci numbers.

The sequence satisfies Binet's formula, a closed form: F of n equals phi to the n minus one minus phi to the n, all divided by the square root of five. Fibonacci numbers are intimately connected to the golden spiral and logarithmic spirals in nature. The sequence has deep connections to number theory. The gcd of F of m and F of n equals F of the gcd of m and n. Fibonacci numbers exhibit divisibility properties. In combinatorics, the number of ways to tile a one-by-n board with one-by-two dominoes equals F of n plus one.

Every positive integer can be uniquely represented as a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers, according to Zeckendorf's theorem. This connects the sequence to number systems. Fibonacci numbers appear in plant phyllotaxis, branching patterns, and seed arrangements, demonstrating nature's preference for mathematical optimization. The generalized Fibonacci sequence with different initial conditions and Lucas numbers provide extensions useful in number theory and algebraic geometry.
